sources.title: Marianne North (Q271648), verified live via the Wikidata API (2026-11-15): English label 'Marianne North', description 'English philanthropist, painter, biologist and botanical artist (1830-1890)', born 1830-10-24, died 1890-08-30, citizen of the United Kingdom, instance of human; no Korean label. Orientation only; not used as support for any row.

'Marianne North', Encyclopedia of World Biography (Gale), read at Encyclopedia.com (about 2,700 words, read in full; it draws on Vision of Eden, 1980, and Notable Women Scientists). CANONICAL SIGNIFICANCE SOURCE: a well-known botanical painter who travelled the world seeking rare plants and painted them in their natural habitats; the gallery she gave to the Royal Botanic Gardens at Kew opened in 1882 and holds 832 paintings made over 13 years; her 1871-1885 journeys (North America and Jamaica, Brazil, Japan, Sarawak, Java, Sri Lanka, India, Australia and New Zealand, South Africa, the Seychelles, Chile); five plants named for her including the giant pitcher plant Nepenthes northiana; her preference for travelling alone, the harsh conditions she minimised in her diaries, and her late years in Gloucestershire. Gale reference biography: admiring in tone but notes that her diaries barely mention the people she met.

Ellen McHale, 'Six things you should know about Marianne North', Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew (read in full, about 900 words). INSTITUTIONAL (Kew houses her gallery): she began solo travel at 40 after her father's death, visited 15 countries in 14 years between 1871 and 1885, used oil paint and painted plants within their habitats rather than in the usual watercolour botanical manner, painted the Bornean pitcher plant later named Nepenthes northiana, used a limited travelling palette, wrote to Joseph Hooker in 1879 offering her paintings and a gallery, chose the site and appointed her friend to design it, and the gallery opened in 1882 with 838 paintings. Celebratory institutional page.

Australian Garden History Society, review of Lorna Howarth-Gladston's 'Marianne North, A Victorian Painter for the 21st Century' (Lund Humphries with Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew, 2024), 'Marianne North: botanical painter and plant hunter' (April 2025; read in full, about 900 words). Independent book review that reports the biography's findings: her mixed reception (admired by some, called gaudy and amateurish by others), the influence of Hunt, Lear, the Hudson River painters, Pre-Raphaelite detail and Humboldt, her introduction to oil painting, Darwin's advice to visit Australia, her comments on introduced species and the clearing of forest, the 1882 gallery arranged by region, the Gardeners' Chronicle review, Hooker's catalogue preface on vanishing habitats, and her sister's remark that she was 'scornfully sceptical as to rules in art'.

Eadaoin Agnew, ''An Old Vagabond': Science and Sexuality in Marianne North's Representations of India', Nineteenth-Century Gender Studies 7.2 (Summer 2011; scholarly article, read for the sections on her travels, her letters, her gallery and her critics). COUNTER-VOICE: documents her letters to Arthur Burnell and Miss Shaen of 1878 (preferring to stay with no one, scorn for hill-station society), the 1879 gallery plan, her deference to Kew and wish to be counted among botanists, her removal of people from her landscapes, her active endorsement of collecting for Kew, and Wilfrid Blunt's harsh verdict on the paintings. Reads her as taking part in imperial natural history. Only her documented conduct is used here; the article's psychoanalytic and sexual readings are not used.

Marianne North, 'Recollections of a Happy Life, being the autobiography of Marianne North', edited by her sister Mrs. John Addington Symonds (London: Macmillan, 1892; Internet Archive scans, OCR text read for the Kew gift, the Sarawak pitcher plant, the 1882-83 African journey, the Chilean trip and the editor's closing note). SELF-REPORT (edited by a sister): her account of offering the paintings and a gallery to Sir Joseph Hooker, his refusal of a refreshment room, choosing the site herself, travelling to Africa and Chile to complete the geographical set, and the sister's note that she fought against increasing weakness to finish the gallery.

Christin Geall, 'Reckoning with Marianne North', Wonderground Press (16 June 2022; essay by a former Kew intern and plant writer, read in full). Modern independent essay on the Kew gallery and her autobiography: her class privilege and use of letters of introduction on her journeys, her indifference to slavery in a quoted passage, her use of oil paint and of ecological associations in her pictures, and the gallery's dense hanging; reads the gallery as a product of an imperial age.

Wikipedia, 'Marianne North' (read; orientation only, never counted as a source and not used as support for any row). It was read to cross-check dates (the 1871-72 North American journey, Brazil, the 1880 Australian trip at Darwin's suggestion, the 1882 gallery opening, death at Alderley in 1890).

persistence.rationale: [src_north_gale, src_north_kew, src_north_recollections | 1871-1886 | reference biography, institutional page, self-report edited by a sister] Between 1871 and 1885 she made journey after journey to fifteen countries (Kew); Gale says she carried on through rheumatic fever in Japan, increasing deafness and failing health, and worked on her Gloucestershire garden in her last years despite poor health; the sister's closing note says she fought against increasing weakness to finish the gallery. The long sequence of journeys is well documented; her endurance of hardship rests partly on her sister's tribute.

autonomy_need.rationale: [src_north_gale, src_north_kew, src_north_agnew, src_north_recollections | 1871-1885 | reference biography, institutional page, scholarly article quoting her letters, self-report] Gale says travelling alone was how she preferred to do it and that she sometimes started a trip with a friend and left them partway; Kew says she travelled almost always on her own; Agnew quotes her 1878 letters saying she was 'delighted to be perfectly free again, staying with no one' and criticising the late hours of hill-station society; she chose the Kew gallery site herself and wanted a room of her own to paint in. Several sources agree, though much of it traces back to her own letters and autobiography. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): lowered from 74 / 0.58 to 70 / 0.52 because the preference for travelling alone and avoiding company is documented mainly by her own letters and autobiography, which Gale, Kew and the scholarly article repeat or quote.

independent_thinking.rationale: [src_north_ghs, src_north_kew, src_north_agnew | 1865-1882 | book review, institutional page, scholarly article] She took up oil paint in about 1865 after a visiting painter introduced it, although oils were not usual in botanical illustration, and kept to oils; her sister called her 'scornfully sceptical as to rules in art' and said she had hardly any artistic teaching; Agnew says she declined to compromise her artistic approach to fit Kew. Contemporary and later critics (Blunt, the book review) found her work gaudy, which she carried on regardless. The sister's remark is the main direct statement.

creative_originality.rationale: [src_north_kew, src_north_ghs, src_north_agnew, src_north_gale | 1871-1885 | institutional page, book review, scholarly article, reference biography] Four sources describe an unusual approach: oil paint on board instead of watercolour botanical plates, plants shown in their habitat with animals, buildings and people, a rapid, vividly coloured manner, and a gallery hung by region in which paintings fill the walls. The same sources record that her reception was mixed, and Agnew quotes Blunt's low view of her paintings, so originality here means departure from convention, not a verdict on quality.

proactive_agency.rationale: [src_north_gale, src_north_kew, src_north_ghs, src_north_agnew, src_north_recollections | 1871-1882 | reference biography, institutional page, book review, scholarly article, self-report] At 41 she sold the family house and set out to paint tropical vegetation, then in 1879 wrote to Joseph Hooker offering her paintings and a gallery built at her own expense, chose the site, hired James Fergusson to design it, arranged the pictures herself and had it open in 1882; she also paid for a catalogue. Five sources give the gallery gift, and Hooker's 1882 catalogue preface (quoted in the book review) thanks her for it. Documented in concrete steps; her own letter is one account of the proposal. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): lowered from 76 / 0.64 to 74 / 0.6 because the offer to Hooker is known chiefly from her own account, which the other sources retell; the physical gallery and Hooker's preface independently show the gift but not how much of the initiative was hers alone (an architect and Kew staff did the building work).

resourcefulness.rationale: [src_north_kew, src_north_gale, src_north_wonderground | 1871-1885 | institutional page, reference biography, modern essay] She kept to a restricted palette to reduce what she had to carry, painted in a hut in the Brazilian forest and, Gale says, often had to pack paintings still wet and touch them up on her return; the essay says she used letters of introduction as tickets for rides, beds and houses. Letters of introduction and hired help (Gale) mean her practical ingenuity was backed by privilege, so the score stays moderate. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): lowered from 66 / 0.5 to 62 / 0.46 because the limited-palette point is hedged by Kew ('it is believed') and the rest rests on Gale's general description and an essay's reading of her autobiography; her letters of introduction and hired helpers did much of the practical work.

risk_tolerance.rationale: [src_north_gale, src_north_kew | 1871-1885 | reference biography, institutional page] She travelled alone to remote places, crossed jungle and swamp and climbed cliffs and mountains in search of plants (Gale), and Kew says her solo travel defied the convention that women should not go unaccompanied. Gale and the essay also note she travelled with servants and letters of introduction, and her diaries make light of the dangers; the sources do not describe how she weighed particular risks, and her health paid for it. dual_edged because her declining health is linked by Gale to the hardships. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): lowered from 64 / 0.46 to 60 / 0.42 because the evidence is indirect (travel to remote places) and the sources agree she travelled with introductions, servants and means, so willingness to accept danger is not directly shown.

curiosity.rationale: [src_north_kew, src_north_agnew, src_north_ghs, src_north_gale | 1850s-1883 | institutional page, scholarly article, book review, reference biography] A flowering Amherstia nobilis given to her at Kew made her long to see the tropics (Kew, Agnew); she went to Australia in 1880 at Darwin's suggestion to see its unusual plants (book review, Gale), travelled to Chile to paint the monkey-puzzle tree because it was missing from her gallery (her autobiography), and questioned how a flower pushed through a honeycomb (Agnew quoting her). Her interest here is directed at plants and places; her own questions are shown only by a few quoted passages. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): lowered from 64 / 0.5 to 62 / 0.48 because her own questions are shown by one quoted passage and the Darwin-suggested Australian trip is known from her account and a book review of a biography; the sources are not independent of her autobiography.

impact_motivation.rationale: [src_north_agnew, src_north_ghs, src_north_gale | 1871-1882 | scholarly article, book review, reference biography] Agnew quotes her saying that she found people 'woefully ignorant of natural history' and that she set out to show them tropical vegetation; she gave the gallery free to Kew, arranged by geographical region so visitors could see the distribution of plants, and Hooker's preface says the paintings record habitats that were disappearing. Her wish to educate the public is documented mainly in her own words and Hooker's preface; the sources show her aims, not how many visitors she changed. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): lowered from 60 / 0.46 to 56 / 0.42 because her educational aim is documented mainly by her own statements quoted by Agnew and by Hooker's preface, which is one contemporary voice.

portrait.source: Photograph of Marianne North standing on the doorstep of her house at Alderley, Gloucestershire, by her neighbour Mrs. Bryan Hodgson, taken soon after North arrived there in 1886 and printed as the frontispiece to volume 2 of Recollections of a Happy Life (London and New York: Macmillan; Internet Archive scan recollectionsofh02nortuoft, University of Toronto copy, Macmillan 1894 printing, whose first edition appeared in 1892). The plate carries North's own handwritten caption 'Marianne North at home, Mount House, Alderley, May to November as long as life lasts'. Her sister's preface states that the frontispiece shows her on the doorstep of her house at Alderley, was done by a neighbour, Mrs. Bryan Hodgson, on her first arrival there, and bears her signature. The file is the Wikimedia Commons extract of the page (1688 x 2904 pixels), cropped to the photograph (caption and margins removed) and downscaled to 696 x 1000, with no upscaling.
portrait.license: Public domain: published in the United Kingdom and the United States in 1892-1894 (before 1931); the Internet Archive record for the scan states possible-copyright-status NOT_IN_COPYRIGHT and no rights of its own; Commons tags the extract PD-1923. The photographer's death date was not established, so the basis is publication date, not creator death.
portrait.attribution: Mrs. Bryan (Susan) Hodgson, photograph of Marianne North at Mount House, Alderley, c. 1886; frontispiece to Recollections of a Happy Life, vol. 2 (Macmillan, 1892; 1894 printing scanned); Internet Archive scan, extracted via Wikimedia Commons and downscaled.
portrait.creator: Mrs. Bryan Hodgson (Susan Hodgson), neighbour at Alderley
portrait.date: c. 1886 (taken soon after she moved to Alderley; published 1892)

provenance.notes: portrait_preflight: STRONG (lead) / REPLACED: the lead's route was Julia Margaret Cameron's 1877 photograph (Commons scan from Colin Ford's 1975 book, 'originally from a private collection'; V&A holds a separate head-and-shoulders print, PH.256-1982, with non-commercial image terms). I opened the Commons file and the V&A record: the Commons scan is a different composition (North at an easel, in profile, with a Tamil boy; no caption) and its first publication appears to be the 1975 book, so its provenance is weaker than the preflight suggested and the face is small; it was not used. The replacement is Mrs Bryan Hodgson's c.1886 photograph of North on her Alderley doorstep, printed as the frontispiece to volume 2 of Recollections of a Happy Life. IDENTITY: the plate carries North's own handwritten caption naming her and Mount House, Alderley, and the editor's preface (read in the Internet Archive OCR) says the frontispiece shows her on her doorstep, by a neighbour Mrs Bryan Hodgson, with her signature. Commons dates the file 'c. 1869', which is wrong (she rented the Alderley house in 1886 per the same book). RIGHTS: published 1892-94, before 1931; Internet Archive record NOT_IN_COPYRIGHT; no holder statement conflicts. KIND likeness (photograph from life). Dimensions 696 x 1000 after crop, downscaled from 1688 x 2904. PREFLIGHT: QID VERIFIED LIVE (2026-11-15, Wikidata API) Q271648 label 'Marianne North', description 'English philanthropist, painter, biologist and botanical artist (1830-1890)', born 1830-10-24, died 1890-08-30, human; no Korean label, so the Korean display name is a transliteration (flagged for lead review). REGION western_europe (English). ERA 19th_century. ATTRIBUTION: attributable (dated journeys, a physical gallery, letters, a contemporary catalogue preface). CANONICAL SIGNIFICANCE SOURCE: Gale Encyclopedia of World Biography entry (via Encyclopedia.com). READ: Gale entry (full), Kew page (full), Australian Garden History Society book review of the 2024 Howarth-Gladston biography (full), Agnew 2011 article (read for her travels, letters, gallery and critics), Recollections volumes 1 and 2 (OCR passages), Wonderground essay (full); Wikipedia and Wikidata for orientation only. Britannica and the Kew gallery pages returned 403 to automated fetches and were not used. NOT OPENED: Howarth-Gladston's book itself, Vision of Eden (1980), Carroll 2017/18 in Third Text (PDF 403), the 2021 Frankfurt study of her Australian paintings (bot wall), the V&A item page itself (V&A API record read). PERSPECTIVES: reference biography; institutional (Kew, self-interested); an independent review of the 2024 biography; a critical scholarly article (Agnew, which reads her as part of imperial natural history and quotes Blunt's low opinion of her paintings); a modern essay; her own autobiography edited by her sister (self). NON-SELF BEHAVIOURAL SOURCES: Gale, the biography review, Agnew's documentation of her letters (self but independent scholarship), Kew. Much of what all of them say about her motives traces to Recollections and her letters, so every row is flagged for single-family concentration. COUNTER-VOICES: Blunt and the review's 'gaudy and amateurish', Agnew's reading of her naming and collecting as part of imperial science, the essay's remark on her indifference to slavery in a quoted passage; none changes a score because rows describe her working conduct only. CONFLICTS NOT CARDED: gallery paintings 832 (Gale) versus 838 (Kew); the date she first wrote to Hooker (1879, Kew, Agnew) versus the gallery opening 1882. Her health, nerves, deafness, family life and views on marriage are not scored. ZERO POLITICS: none.
